1:
The form of the psalm is described before anything in it. Keil and Delitzsch set out the arithmetic, a hundred and seventy-six verses falling into twenty-two groups of eight after the letters of the alphabet, each verse of a group beginning with the same letter, and they gather what the old authorities called it: the Latin psalters printed the name of the letter before each group and one Syriac copy the letter-signs, the Talmud said it consists of eight Alephs, and the Masora and the later commentaries each had a name for it as the great alphabet. Adam Clarke gives the same scheme and draws a consequence from it, that all connection is sacrificed, as might naturally be expected, to so artificial and methodical an arrangement. He also lists the ten words by which the revelation is named here — testimonies, commandments, precepts, word, law, ways, truth, judgments, righteousness and statutes — notes that some would add three more, and reports the almost universal claim that one or other of the ten stands in every verse but a single exception, before saying that closer inspection modifies it.

Whether the psalm has any order is therefore the first question, and it is argued on both sides inside one block. John Calvin says it is difficult to epitomise, that the writer passes from topic to topic and prosecutes none continuously, though two aims run through it. The paragraph attached to his block then names the parties: it has been too commonly assumed, one writer objects, that the psalm is a collection of unconnected thoughts, an opinion toward which even a profound religious philosopher inclined, whose eloquent words must in this instance be received with no small caution — and that philosopher’s own description is given, of manifold reflections and sprightly ejaculations conceived in different forms of speech, some by way of petition, some of thanksgiving, some of resolution, some of aphorism, not ranged in any strict order but like a variety of wholesome herbs. C.H. Spurgeon takes the opposite view from within: there is no tautology here and no thought repeated, though to the careless reader it may seem so, and he traces the changes rung on three words through the eight verses. He also notes the manner rather than the matter, that prayer and praise and all sorts of devotional feeling gleam through the verses like beams of sunlight through an olive grove.

On the blessedness promised, Augustine of Hippo makes the offer conditional in a sentence: I know what thou wishest, thou art seeking bliss, and if thou wouldest be blessed, be undefiled; the first all desire and the second all fear, yet without the second the first cannot be had. He adds that the workers of wickedness do search these testimonies, but for the reason that they prefer being learned to being righteous. Matthew Henry keeps a school running through his notes, that we must be scholars in Christ’s school as long as we live but should aim to be head-scholars, and that though he teaches without money he expects thanks; and he warns that it will not serve to make religion the subject of our discourse, since it must be the rule of our walk. Charles Ellicott reads the sixth verse as a mirror in which the law shows a man his defects, so that the faithful looking into it have no cause to blush. Clarke presses the totality, that if any one commandment may be transgressed the whole ten are soon set aside, and that God has never given a command he knew to be impossible. John Gill and John Wesley both narrow the third verse to the will, Gill by referring the sinlessness to the new creature and Wesley by defining respect as allowing oneself in no known sin.
9:
The opening question is famous, and Charles Ellicott disputes what counts as its answer. He would render it, by what means can a young man purify his way so as to keep it according to thy word, which makes the word the standard reached rather than the means used; and he holds that no direct answer is given at all, the reply being left to be inferred from the whole tenor of the psalm, that men can do nothing of themselves and depend on grace. The omission, he adds, rather strengthens than impairs the impression on the reader. The others supply the answer the received rendering suggests. Matthew Henry widens the question first, asking by what means the next generation may be made better than this, and observes that few young people ask it for themselves, so the psalmist asks it for them; his answer is that making the word the rule will do more toward cleansing them than the laws of princes or the morals of philosophers. C.H. Spurgeon analyses the difficulty in two directions, since the way must be cleansed of sins already behind and kept clear of those temptation will set in front. John Wesley quietly universalises the subject, that any man is meant and the young man named only because such are commonly void of wisdom and experience. Adam Clarke gets a picture out of the noun, which means a track or rut such as a cart wheel makes: a young sinner has no broad beaten path but his own private ways of offence.

Clarke then does something done nowhere else in this psalm, running a single numbered programme straight through all eight verses. It begins with considering that one’s way is impure and examining it by God’s word, goes on to keeping guard over the general course of life, to seeking God in earnest prayer, to giving the whole heart since any affection kept back for the idol makes prayer useless, to treasuring up the portions of scripture that speak against uncleanness, to acknowledging mercy already shown, to asking God to become one’s teacher, to declaring his judgments even to one’s companions in iniquity, to counting obedience the chief happiness, to self-examination, to keeping the eye on the Saviour’s steps and going and doing and keeping company only where he would, and to never forgetting either what God has done or what one has promised. Fifteen particulars in all, and Clarke closes by promising that whoever attends to them will have his way cleansed and victory over his sin.

On hiding the word in the heart they converge, and Henry gives the reason best: it is a treasure worth laying up, and there is no laying it up safely anywhere else, for if we have it only in our houses and hands enemies may take it from us, and if only in our heads our memories may fail. John Gill and Wesley both call it a choice treasure laid up for use on all occasions, and Ellicott notes that it is hidden as treasure was hidden in that country. Ellicott also finds the self-mistrust of the tenth verse a proof of the reality of its first clause, comparing the man who asked help for his unbelief in the act of professing belief. Henry and Ellicott independently reach for the same figure at the thirteenth verse, of the householder bringing out of his store things new and old. Clarke ends on the verb of the last verse, which he says means to skip about and jump for joy. Keil and Delitzsch state the stanza’s argument in one line, that a young man walks blamelessly by acting in accordance with the word of God, which the poet desires and for which he asks assistance.
17:
Adam Clarke finds a joke in the first word of the stanza. The verb rendered deal bountifully is the root from which the name of the third Hebrew letter comes, and that letter heads every verse here, so that the section opens by naming its own initial; this he calls a stroke of the psalmist’s art and ingenuity. C.H. Spurgeon reads the stanzas as successive characters: in the last eight verses the speaker prayed as a youth newly come into the world, and here he pleads as a servant and a pilgrim who finds himself increasingly a stranger in an enemy’s country. On the plea itself Spurgeon notices what its wording excludes, since to ask bounty rather than reward shuts out any idea of legal claim — let my wages be according to thy goodness, not according to my merit. Matthew Henry turns the request outward, that life is a mercy chiefly because it is an opportunity of obeying God, so that the prayer is not to live and grow rich but to live and keep the word.

On the prayer to have the eyes opened, Clarke makes a remark against his own trade: the scriptures are plain enough, but the heart of man is darkened by sin, so that the Bible does not so much need a comment as the soul needs the light of the Spirit. Charles Ellicott puts the same point as an image, that without grace the eyes are veiled to the wonder and beauty of the moral law, and John Gill that the veil must be removed before spiritual things can be discerned even by good men. Henry adds that those who at first saw men as trees walking may come to see clearly, and that the more the eyes are opened the more wonders appear. But the following verse divides them. Ellicott holds that the general transitory condition of life is meant and not any particular circumstance of the writer’s history, since the mortal is a stranger on earth and lacks both time and strength for the knowledge only God can teach. Clarke reads it historically instead, of a man obliged to wander from place to place and so a stranger in his own country, or of captives who after seventy years still felt themselves in exile. Henry gets the force from the speaker’s station, that here was a man who knew the world as well as most and was as well known in it, and who nonetheless called himself a stranger. John Wesley makes it a pilgrimage travelled homeward.

The word for the soul breaking is a crux, and the two textual voices attack it differently. Ellicott reports that the Hebrew occurs in only one other place and gives five ancient renderings of it — greatly desired, was perfect, had confidence, longed — concluding that they point either to a different reading or to a different sense from the one the lexicons give. Clarke does not consult a version at all but reaches for English usage, observing that we say a thing broke my heart, or that a woman died of a broken heart, and that the phrase expresses excessive longing, grievous disappointment and hopeless love. On the next verse Ellicott prefers the older division of the clauses, which makes the curse a separate statement, while Clarke reports manuscripts reading strangers or the heathen in place of the proud. Gill canvasses three candidates for those proud ones, the angels who would not be subject to the Son, the teachers rebuked in the Gospels, or simply all profane persons; Henry finds something of pride at the bottom of every wilful sin. Keil and Delitzsch state the stanza’s aim in a line, that this is his life’s purpose, held under fear of the curse of apostasy and held though he suffer persecution for it.
25:
What the soul cleaving to the dust means is answered five ways. Adam Clarke would translate the noun as my life and take the phrase for an apprehension of approaching death, which he thinks agrees best with the petition that follows; John Wesley says the same, that the speaker is in danger of present death and like one laid in the grave. Charles Ellicott agrees that the dust of death is prominently in view, though he allows that one might otherwise think of the dryness of summer dust as a type of despondency. Matthew Henry offers corruption or affliction, the inclination to the world and the body being both dust. Keil and Delitzsch read it socially, of a man fixed to the ground by non-recognition and proscription and incapable of raising himself. C.H. Spurgeon takes all of them together: mourners in that country cast dust on their heads, and these ensigns of woe felt glued to him; he was half choked by the death-dust; and he bemoaned an earthly-mindedness that clung to him. Spurgeon also plays the English alphabet against the Hebrew one, observing that this portion has D for its letter and sings of depression in the spirit of devotion, determination and dependence.

The verb of the twenty-eighth verse divides the textual readings from the vernacular ones. John Gill has the soul melting like wax before the fire or flowing like water, and Clarke that the word means to distil or drop as tears from the eye, so that affliction makes the life ebb and leak out. Ellicott traces the same word to a dripping house-roof in one book and to weeping in another, but then reports that the older versions render it slumbered, and holds that this suits far better with the next clause, which is literally make me rise up. On the opening verse Ellicott adds two things nobody else has: a modern poet’s line that God will not leave us in the dust, and another’s about a wicked whisper that made the heart as dry as dust; and the record that an emperor recited this verse when doing penance at the door of a cathedral for a massacre. He also reads the reiterated prayer for quickening as the petition of a nation for revived covenant glory, while granting it a wide field of individual application.

On the way of lying two of them flatly contradict each other. Henry takes it of plain untruth and says the speaker was conscious of a proneness to that very sin, naming two occasions on which he had deceived men in a strait; great difficulties, Henry adds, are great temptations to palliate a lie with the colour of a pious fraud and necessary self-defence. Gill denies the whole basis, holding that the sin of lying to men was not one to which the speaker was addicted, and reads the phrase instead of a false way, meaning false doctrine and false worship, error, superstition and idolatry. Ellicott stands between them, making it insincerity toward God rather than falsehood to men. On the choosing of the next verse Henry insists the choice must be deliberate and made not because no other way is known but because none better is, since the choosing Christian is likely to be the steady one while those who are Christians by chance tack about if the wind turn; and he compares laying the judgments before oneself to a learner setting out his copy or a workman his model. Clarke notices the stanza’s own echo, that the word for sticking to the testimonies is the same as the word for the soul cleaving to the dust, so that the one clinging answers the other.
33:
Matthew Henry notices the order the stanza follows. The earlier prayer was that the understanding be enlightened so that duty might be known; here the prayer is that the will be bowed and the active powers quickened so that duty may be done, both the good head and the good heart being necessary and both from the same grace. He adds that it is as good to have no understanding at all as to have it unsanctified, and that the spirit of revelation in the word will not answer its end without the spirit of wisdom in the heart. Adam Clarke makes the same request narrower and harder: to understand the spiritual reference of all the statutes required a teaching that could come only from God, asked not to make a parade of it but to discern duty. John Gill grants that the law cannot be kept perfectly by any mere man but holds it may be kept spiritually, from love and gratitude. Charles Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch both note that the little adverb rendered to the end is peculiar to this psalm; Keil and Delitzsch add that the stanza prays for guidance out of the by-paths of selfishness and disavowal, and Ellicott gets a picture from the word for path, which comes from a root meaning to tread and so means the trodden way, plain with the track of all the pious feet of past times.

On the eyes and what they must not rest on, two of them suspect idolatry. Ellicott suggests that the vanity may be idols, and Clarke lists an idol first among worldly pleasure, beauty and finery, then supplies a warning in four verbs: remember the man who saw, coveted, took, hid his theft, and was slain for his sin. Henry works the same danger as a physics of attention, that the eye fastened on such things infects the heart with the love of them, so that we ought to make a covenant with our eyes; and he observes that beholding vanity deadens us and slackens our pace, since a traveller who stands gazing at every object in view will not get over ground. On the covetousness named in the preceding verse John Wesley explains why it should be singled out, as most opposite to the testimonies, most common a hindrance to receiving the word, and most pernicious as the root of all evil; Ellicott makes the word harsher still, rendering it literally rapine or prey.

The fear of reproach at the close draws the sharpest disagreement in the stanza. Gill reports two Jewish commentators referring it to the speaker’s own recorded sins in a notorious case, lest they should be a perpetual reproach on his name and family. Henry says the same in his own terms, that the speaker was conscious of having given occasion to blaspheme. Clarke gives the general sense first, that a godly life was never fashionable in any time or country, and then quotes an unattributed note he had found which reads the verse as a private confession — I have done a secret evil, my soul is sorry for it, and if it become public it will be a heavy reproach; O God, turn it away and let it never meet the eye of man. Ellicott takes the opposite view, allowing the disgrace of violating the commands but preferring, on the evidence of the next verse, a reproach suffered from men for keeping the law. On the preceding verse Ellicott rejects the received rendering outright, calling the usual explanation of the elliptical phrase improbable and offering two others, while Henry builds an entire character of the good man upon the reading Ellicott discards. Henry ends with a rule worth the stanza: what God has promised we must pray for, and we need not be so aspiring as to ask more nor so modest as to ask less.
41:
The plural of the opening word is noticed by two of them. C.H. Spurgeon says the speaker needed much mercy and varied mercy, and that the request is therefore in the plural; he desires mercy as well as teaching because he was guilty as well as ignorant. Keil and Delitzsch secure the same plural against the Greek version, which has the singular, on the authority of two other ancient renderings, and read the stanza as a prayer for the grace of a true and fearlessly joyous confession. The answer promised to the reviler is read by Charles Ellicott as a piece of word-play: rendering the clause literally, I shall answer my reviler a word, he takes the sense to be that when reproached it will be enough simply to pronounce God’s promise, and he supports this from the repetition of the same noun in the next verse. John Gill supplies the taunt being answered, that there is no help for him in God, and Adam Clarke that many say his hope in mercy is vain.

On walking at liberty they agree in substance and differ in ground. Matthew Henry makes it a paradox: the service of sin is perfect slavery and the service of God perfect liberty, so that licentiousness is bondage to the greatest of tyrants and conscientiousness freedom to the meanest of prisoners. Ellicott renders it literally in a large place. Gill takes the same phrase as walking at large or in a broad way, and immediately guards it, since the broad way meant is not the one leading to destruction but the law of God, which is exceeding broad. Clarke alone reads it politically, as what will be enjoyed when the present bondage is over.

Whose courts are meant, when the speaker undertakes to talk of the testimonies before kings, divides them along the same line as the psalm’s date. Gill names the courts of the speaker’s own youth and the visiting kings of his later reign. Henry says the same, that before he came to the crown kings were sometimes his judges. Clarke reports a scholar who referred the verse to a particular foreign king whom the psalmist had instructed in his religion, rejects it because he holds the psalm compiled during the captivity, and refers the words instead to those who spoke courageously before the kings of that exile. Ellicott leaves the question and records what became of the verse: the old Latin of it, following the Greek in its tenses, was taken as the motto of a famous confession of faith. Clarke turns the same verse into a rebuke of his own readers, that it is a shame to Christians to feel so little affection for the Gospel when such cordial and inviolate attachment appears here in a Jew toward ordinances that afforded not a thousandth part of the privileges. On the lifting of the hands at the close, four senses are offered: Gill takes the gesture for esteem, for prayer, for an oath and for setting the hand to the work; Clarke for sacrifice and supplication; Ellicott supplies the ellipsis as lifting the hands in prayer for power to observe the commands; and John Wesley makes it a gesture of receiving and embracing. Henry reads the whole stanza as a prayer for the tongue of the learned, so that a man may never be afraid or ashamed to own the truth when called upon.
49:
C.H. Spurgeon catches the exact shape of the opening plea: the speaker does not say remember my service to thee but thy word to me, and asks for no new promise, only that the old one be fulfilled. He adds a wry observation, that the words of masters to servants are not always such that servants wish them remembered, since they usually record the faults of work not answering the command. Matthew Henry puts the same as a rule, that those who make God’s promises their portion may with humble boldness make them their plea. Adam Clarke reads the promise as one of release from captivity. On the word rendered comfort in the next verse, Charles Ellicott notes it occurs in only one other place in the language, and would repunctuate the line so that the comfort consists precisely in the quickening.

The derision reported next is described most vividly by Henry, who lists the jeers: they laughed at his praying and called it cant, at his seriousness and called it mopishness, at his strictness and called it needless preciseness. His answer is that a traveller goes on his way though the dogs bark at him, and that those can bear little for Christ who cannot bear a hard word for him; the speaker had not merely refused to forsake the law but had not so much as declined from it. John Gill makes the derided man a type of one later derided by the same class of scorners. On the judgments remembered against that derision they divide. Gill offers either the judgments executed on the wicked, instancing the flood, the overthrow of the cities and the drowning of the pursuing host, or the providential dealings with God’s own people. Clarke takes the word here for providential dealing and indeed for kind treatment, while John Wesley takes it strictly of ancient dispensations in punishing the ungodly.

The word rendered horror sends three of them to the same desert wind and two of them to opposite emotions. Clarke says the noun is thought to signify the pestilential burning wind of the Arabs, and takes it for horror at the destructive nature of sin, which is pestilential and mortal. Ellicott names the same wind and renders the word violent indignation, a storm of rage; Keil and Delitzsch agree, describing the speaker as burning with indignation at the apostates. Gill keeps the storm without deciding, and Wesley calls it a mixed passion of abhorrence, dread and sorrow. Henry locates its cause precisely, that the fright was not at the designs against him but at the contempt put upon God. On the house of pilgrimage Gill canvasses four senses, a fugitive’s unsettled state, a palace regarded as an inn, the body as a tabernacle, or best of all the whole course of life; and he supports the last from two ancient philosophers who called this life a kind of pilgrimage. Clarke again reads captivity, and again Ellicott weighs that reading and sets it aside, allowing a possible reference to exile but preferring the transitoriness of human life; his own rendering is that the statutes were music in the house of the speaker’s sojournings. Henry supplies the picture, of travellers diverting the tedium of a journey by singing as they go, and closes the stanza with a maxim: God’s work is its own wages, and a heart to obey his will is itself a most valuable reward of obedience.
57:
The first sentence is broken in the Hebrew, and three of them notice it. C.H. Spurgeon says the translators have mended it by insertions and that it had perhaps been better left alone, standing as the exclamation, my portion, O Lord; the poet is lost in wonder that the great God is all his own, and rejoices like one seizing his share of a divided spoil. Charles Ellicott mends it the other way, and reverses the sense in doing so: a better rendering, he holds, would make the portion not God himself but the keeping of his words. Keil and Delitzsch take the same side, that to understand and keep God’s word is his portion and the highest favour that can come to him. Matthew Henry builds a whole character on the received reading instead, that a godly man makes the favour of God his felicity and must take him for his prince as well as for his portion.

Adam Clarke does something here he does nowhere else in the psalm: he rearranges the verses. He treats the whole composition as notes selected from diaries of past experience formed at different times, and holds that the author was obliged, for the support of his acrostic plan, to put behind what in the order of grace comes before, since otherwise the letters would not fall into their alphabetical order; and so Clarke announces that he will follow what he conceives to be the order of grace rather than the order of the words. He then renumbers the stanza into seven steps: first the thinking on one’s ways, then the turning of the feet, then the making haste, then the entreating of favour with the whole heart, then the plea for mercy according to the word, then the binding of oneself by a promise, and last the discovery that God is the portion — so that the stanza ends where the text begins. On the third of these he is delighted by the Hebrew, which he says is amazingly emphatical and means that the man did not stand what-what-whating, or, as we should say, shilly-shallying with himself. On the first he takes the verb for a metaphor from embroidery, in which the figure must appear the same on both sides so that the cloth is turned at every stitch to see it fairly set; Henry independently reaches the same figure, of workers in embroidery careful to cover the least flaw, or else of men casting up accounts, and adds that the speaker thought not on his wealth but on his ways, since what we do follows us into another world while what we have must be left behind.

Whether the wicked robbed him or merely surrounded him is disputed. John Gill follows the received sense and supplies three occasions of plunder from the speaker’s history, while reporting that one Jewish commentator rejects that sense of the word and renders it took hold of me. Ellicott agrees with the rejection and says all the ancient versions but one read that the cords of the wicked surrounded him. Clarke keeps the cords but makes them snares, saying they have hunted us like wild beasts. On the midnight thanksgiving Henry notes the reverence of it, that the man rose out of his bed, perhaps in the cold and the dark, to do it the more solemnly, and that he was a good husband of time, since when he could not lie and sleep he would rise and pray; and Henry adds that public worship will not excuse us from secret. Gill recalls two prisoners who sang at the same hour. On the companionship of the last verses Henry observes that though the speaker was a king he would associate with the poorest of his subjects who feared God, and John Wesley that the injuries done him were done for his respect to the law.
65:
Four of them arrive at the same rendering of the thing asked for in the sixty-sixth verse, and it is not judgment but taste. Matthew Henry says the word signifies a good taste, a good relish, by which things that differ are discerned, since the ear tries words as the mouth tastes meat, and adds that many have knowledge who have little judgment. Adam Clarke renders it a good taste and discernment, and a relish for divine things. John Gill expands the same figure at length, since as the taste discerns perverse things in food, so a man of spiritual taste distinguishes good from evil and truth from error. Charles Ellicott agrees that it is more exactly good taste, though in a moral and not an artistic sense, and suggests that tact or delicate moral perception comes nearest. C.H. Spurgeon treats the stanza as a sermon on its own opening line, calling the first verse the text of the entire eight; Ellicott makes a larger observation of the same kind, that it is characteristic of this psalm that the higher the conception of the divine nature rises, the more earnest becomes the prayer for knowledge of God’s will in relation to conduct.

On the confession that the speaker went astray before he was afflicted, they draw different lessons. Henry blames prosperity, which makes people conceited of themselves, indulgent of the flesh, forgetful of God, in love with the world and deaf to the reproofs of the word; and he ends with the son whose distress brought him first to himself and then to his father. Clarke compresses the whole into an epigram, that affliction sanctified is a great blessing and affliction unsanctified an additional curse. Gill takes care to acquit the speaker of anything wilful, since the straying was not through contempt but through weakness and a careless and negligent frame of spirit, so that he wandered before he was well aware; the word, he notes, is used of erring through ignorance. Ellicott alone reads the verse historically, and with unusual confidence, holding it beyond much doubt that the exile and its moral effect on the nation are alluded to. Clarke says the same of the lie forged in the following verse, that the captives had their conduct and motives continually misrepresented.

That forged lie is a piece of needlework in the original, and two of them see it. Gill renders the verb as sewing a lie to him, fastening one on him or stitching one lie to another; Ellicott gives it as patched, notes that the verb occurs only twice elsewhere, and compares a Greek and a Latin idiom for stitching deceit, adding a line from a play in which one character tells another that he patched up his excuses. On the fat heart that follows, four of them converge on insensibility rather than luxury: Gill compares creatures grown too fat to have feeling, Clarke says they are brutalized in the flesh and have no spiritual relish, John Wesley calls them stupid and insensible, and Henry that they are past feeling and not sensible of the touch of the word or the rod. Keil and Delitzsch state the stanza’s doctrine plainly, that the good word of the gracious God is the fountain of all good and is learned in the way of lowliness, the speaker reviewing his life and seeing in everything that befell him the well-meaning appointment of the God of salvation.
73:
C.H. Spurgeon opens with a joke at the expense of the governing letter, remarking that though every verse here begins with it, the section certainly does not treat of jots and titles and other trifles. On the two verbs of the first line three of them notice a double act. Spurgeon says the maker was doubly thoughtful, being represented as both making and moulding, and as manifesting love and wisdom in giving existence and in arranging it. Adam Clarke divides them the same way, the first forming the mass and the second giving the particular form that distinguishes this creature from all others; he then turns the fact into a request, that having been raised above the beasts in form and mode of life he may be taught to live for a nobler end, and shown that he was made for heaven and not for earth. Charles Ellicott glosses the second verb literally as fixed or established. Matthew Henry presses the doctrine that every man is as truly the work of God’s hands as the first man was, and makes the argument of the verse explicit: God made us to serve and enjoy him, and by sin we have made ourselves unable for both, so that the maker must make again. Keil and Delitzsch state the same inference, that it is impossible God should forsake a man who is his own creature and deny him the one thing that makes him truly happy.

On the confession that the affliction was faithful, Henry marks the difficulty exactly: it is easier to own in general that God’s judgments are right than to own it when the case is one’s own, and the speaker subscribes to it with application, that even his own afflictions are just and kind. John Gill softens the corrections into things done with moderation and gentleness and to answer the best purposes, and John Wesley makes them pursuant to the promises and directed to the sufferer’s good. Henry adds that afflictions are inside the covenant and therefore not merely not meant for our hurt but really intended for our good. On the kindness asked for next, Henry observes that a good man cannot live with any satisfaction longer than he has some token of God’s favour, and Clarke that the comfort sought is a diffusion of exuberant goodness through the soul.

Two things are asked about other people, and the second is the harder. When the proud are to be ashamed, Henry and Gill both give the request two possible ends, that the shame may be either repentance or ruin, and Gill adds a third, the mere confusion of men who fail of their purpose. But when those who fear God are asked to turn to the speaker, the request implies that they had turned away. Gill says plainly that some good men had left him and sided with his enemies, and reports two Jewish commentators referring this to the aftermath of the affair with another man’s wife, when those who feared the Lord would no longer keep him company. Henry reaches the same conclusion independently, that after that foul sin those who feared God grew strange to him and turned from him, king though he was. Clarke reads the verse the opposite way, as men seeing God’s work in him and acknowledging him a brand plucked from the burning. Ellicott finds in the earlier verse of the pair the latent truth of spiritual communion, and observes that in its plainest sense, that the deliverance of persecuted righteous men gladdens all truly good ones, the verse has been amply confirmed by history.
81:
C.H. Spurgeon places the stanza in the architecture of the whole: this octave is the midnight of the psalm, and very dark and black it is, though stars shine out and the last verse gives promise of the dawn. Charles Ellicott observes that the verbs of the first two verses are the same word in Hebrew, and then departs from everyone else on its sense: the failing of the eyes here is the effort of straining to catch or keep sight of a distant object, and not, as so often elsewhere, an exhaustion brought on by sickness or grief; he compares a line from a play in which a watcher would have broken his eye-strings to keep a departing figure in view. John Gill, Adam Clarke and Matthew Henry all read weariness instead, the eyes worn out with long looking for a promise deferred. Keil and Delitzsch note that the word for the speaker’s longing and the word for his enemies’ attempt to finish him are nearly the same, so that his desire and their design are described in one sound.

The bottle in the smoke is the crux of the stanza. Four of them take it for shrivelling: Gill and Clarke explain that bottles there were made of skins, which hung above a fire would parch and shrink; John Wesley says his natural moisture is dried and burnt up; and Henry draws the picture out, that a man once of ruddy countenance is now withered, his colour gone and his cheeks furrowed, and that such a bottle, once wrinkled, is thrown by as a vessel in which there is no pleasure. Henry then qualifies the complaint with unusual candour, that good men when drooping and melancholy sometimes think themselves more slighted than they really are. Ellicott canvasses four possibilities and rejects the easiest. It cannot mean merely that the bottle was set aside, since any bottle in an ancient house would be in the smoke, and that is too weak. It may be misery, as the translators assumed. But the ancient poets mention mellowing wine by heat, and on that reading the image would signify the good results of the discipline of suffering — the exact reverse of the received sense. And since two old versions read hoar-frost for smoke, and the word for bottle can mean a cloud, the whole may be only another expression for weeping.

Clarke returns here to the claim he made at the psalm’s opening, that one of the ten names for the law stands in every verse, and records an exception: in the eighty-fourth verse there is none of them. On the following verse he reports that four ancient versions give a wholly different sentence, in which the proud recite unholy fables rather than dig pits, and he adds an old English rendering that agrees with them. Ellicott makes a small grammatical correction to the same verse with a large effect, that the relative refers to the men and not to the pits, so that it is the diggers and not their diggings that are said to be against the law — where Henry had expressly made the pits themselves the thing contrary to it. On the question how many the days of the servant are, Henry offers both that they are few, so that God should make haste, and that the days of affliction are many; Ellicott reads it corporately, as the dread of each generation lest it pass away before the day of deliverance arrives; and Clarke, as elsewhere in this psalm, asks whether the pride of the captors will not be brought down.
89:
C.H. Spurgeon marks the change of weather at the stanza’s opening: in the former section the speaker’s soul fainted, and here he looks out of himself and perceives that the Lord does not faint, so that after tossing on a sea of trouble the singer leaps ashore and stands upon a rock. He turns the word settled into a rebuke of his own age, since man’s teachings change so often that there is never time for them to be settled, and some men are never happier than when they are unsettling everything and everybody, but God’s mind is not with them. Matthew Henry divides the settling into two, the secret counsel hidden in God and far above out of our sight, immovable as mountains of brass, and the revealed will, which is as firm as the secret one. Keil and Delitzsch put it as a property taken from a place: the word has heaven as its standing-place, and therefore has the qualities of heaven, and before all others a heaven-like stability.

The proof offered is the constancy of nature, and two of them supply the inventory. John Gill lists what has not altered: the heavenly bodies keep the same motion, magnitude, distance and influence, the sun rises and sets as it did, the moon keeps her appointed seasons of increase and decrease, the fixed stars retain their place and the planets their exact revolutions, while on earth seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter follow as before. Henry describes the earth holding still in spite of everything that might move it, poised with its own weight, notwithstanding the convulsions in its own bowels, the agitations of the sea interwoven with it and the concussions of the atmosphere surrounding it. On the verse that states this the two textual voices differ about which clause is the reason. Adam Clarke would invert the order and read that all are God’s servants and therefore continue this day according to his ordinances; Charles Ellicott keeps the received order, makes the all mean the whole universe, and defends the arrangement on the ground that the parallelism is preserved by it and lost by the alternative.

On the short claim in the ninety-fourth verse Henry makes a fine distinction, borrowed from an older writer whom he names: the speaker does not say thou art mine, though that follows of course, because it would be the higher challenge, but I am thine, in a humbler way of resignation; nor does he say I am thus, pleading some quality of his own, but I am thine, pleading God’s property in him. Clarke draws the practical force from it, that he who can say this need fear no evil, and turns it into an appeal that God should save his own. The last verse produces the finest thing in the stanza. Henry reads it as a survey of four undone excellences, and names them from the speaker’s own history: the strongest man overcome, the swiftest overtaken, the wisest befooled and the fairest deformed — poor perfection, he says, which one sees an end of. He adds that the creature fails both in sufficiency and in continuance, since it will not last our time, let alone to eternity as we must. Gill allows the verb a present sense as well, that the most perfect things will have an end and that the end of them is at hand. John Wesley keeps the contrast bare, that the heaven and the earth stand as God appointed them.
97:
Matthew Henry begins with a puzzle about the speaker’s education. In his youth he minded business in the country as a shepherd, and afterwards in the court and camp; by what route then could he come by any great stock of learning? The verses answer it, that he had it from God as author and by the commandments as means. C.H. Spurgeon finds the same answer working in a circle: meditation was both the effect of love and its cause, since he meditated because he loved and then loved the more because he meditated. It is said of some men, Spurgeon adds, that the more you know them the less you admire them, but with this book familiarity breeds affection and affection seeks greater familiarity. Adam Clarke makes the delight itself the evidence, one of the strongest marks of a gracious heart being that it makes the precepts the frequent subject of its thoughts.

The three comparisons that follow — wiser than enemies, than teachers, than the aged — embarrass some of the older readers, and Charles Ellicott explains why. The rabbinical writers disliked the idea of a scholar professing wisdom above his teachers, and so rendered the clause as saying that from all his teachers he got wisdom; which was, Ellicott observes drily, far more in keeping with the process by which their own great commentary grew into existence. John Gill reports the same manoeuvre at the following verse and declines it, preferring the bolder sense; and at the verse about teachers he offers two escapes of his own, either that the teachers meant were bad ones, or that scholars do sometimes exceed their masters, which is no reproach to a master, and he names two such pairs. On the third comparison Ellicott holds it more probable, with the older versions generally, that the word means old men rather than antiquity, and Gill and Keil and Delitzsch take it the same way. Keil and Delitzsch draw a historical inference from the vocabulary, that there were then teachers and elders forming a recognisable class.

Clarke reports here a candidate for the psalm’s authorship that fits his own dating of it, that some have thought it composed by the exile who was found to have more knowledge than all the wise men of the court that held him; and then two verses later he says that the same claim was most literally true of David, who spoke more fully of Christ than any before or after him, and whose compositions Clarke almost calls a sublime Gospel. On the sweetness of the words Gill notes that speech may be tasted and eaten not only in the language of scripture but in that of the classical writers. Clarke turns the verse into his second rebuke of his own readers in this psalm, asking what deep communion the writer must have had, and lamenting that Christians whose privileges are vastly superior have consolations and heavenly-mindedness so vastly inferior. Henry draws a different conclusion from the same comparisons, that the written word is a surer guide to heaven than all the fathers, the teachers and the ancients of the church, and adds that a good man carries his Bible with him wherever he goes, if not in his hands then in his head and heart. John Wesley reduces the stanza’s argument to a line, that the practice of religion is the best way to understand it.
105:
The lamp of the opening verse is made exact by C.H. Spurgeon, who supplies the practice behind it. There being no fixed lamps in eastern towns, each passenger in old times carried a lantern so that he might not fall into the open sewer or stumble over the heaps that defiled the road; and that, he says, is a true picture of our path through this dark world. He draws the moral from the noun rather than the verb: the word is not sent to astound us with its brilliance but to guide us by its instruction, and though the head needs illumination the feet need direction more, else head and feet may both fall into a ditch. Matthew Henry makes the same distinction, that it must be not merely a light to our eyes to fill our heads with speculations but a light to our feet. Two of them notice that the verse names two scales of light. Adam Clarke has a candle that may be held in the hand to light a dark chamber, and also a general light shining on all God’s works; Keil and Delitzsch call the word his torch and his sun. Charles Ellicott adds only a modern poet’s phrase for duty, that it is a light to guide.

The oath of the next verse is deflated by one and enlarged by another. Clarke says it perhaps means no more than that the man had renewed his covenant with God. Henry takes it at full strength and generalises it, that it is good for us to bind ourselves by a solemn oath to be religious, swearing to the Lord as subjects swear allegiance to a sovereign and owning ourselves liable to the curse if we fail. John Gill notes that the verb may equally be rendered as already performed rather than as a promise, and Ellicott connects it with a verb met earlier in the psalm meaning to strengthen or confirm. On the freewill offerings that follow, Ellicott, John Wesley and Henry all take them simply for thanks and praise, the calves of the lips; Clarke alone gives them a historical setting, as the plea of men in captivity who cannot sacrifice but would if they could, and who ask that the praises of their mouths be accepted instead of the offerings they cannot bring to an altar.

On the soul carried continually in the hand Clarke supplies two classical parallels for the idiom, one from a writer preserved in an old compilation who speaks of having the life in the hand, and one from the speech of a Greek hero who says he is always presenting his life to the dangers of the fight. He then reports that four ancient versions read my soul is in thy hand, and dismisses this in four words as a conjectural and useless emendation — a bluntness he uses nowhere else in the psalm. Henry keeps the received reading and finds three senses in it, that every man’s life is thus exposed, that a soldier’s is more so, and that a persecuted good man’s is most of all. Ellicott simply refers the figure to two places where it is used of peril. Gill notices that what is carried in the hands may easily fall or be taken away, and Henry that what we hold, being sandy as our life is, slips of itself through the fingers.
113:
The first word of the stanza is read four different ways. Matthew Henry and C.H. Spurgeon keep the received sense and take it of thoughts, Henry noting that a good man makes conscience of his thoughts since they are words to God, and that vain ones open the door to all evil however lightly they are counted. Adam Clarke makes the noun a class of men and the statement a political one: he has hated tumultuous and violent men, and abominates all mobs and insurrections and troublers of the public peace. Charles Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch converge on a third and narrower sense, that the word means men who halt between two opinions; Ellicott thinks of those inclined for political reasons toward foreign customs who would not throw in their lot with the national party, and Keil and Delitzsch of men doing homage partly to the true worship and partly to heathenism and so trying to combine faith with naturalism. Spurgeon meanwhile turns the received sense against his own decade, remarking that we hear much in these days of men of thought and thoughtful preachers and modern thought, and asking what this is but the old pride of the human heart, since what was called thought in the psalmist’s day was a thing he detested.

On the two images of the following verse Clarke assigns each its occasion, that there is a time when a man is called to suffer in secret and is then hidden, and a time when he is called to fight and is then shielded. Henry gives the pair a longer list of parallels and adds that good people may by faith retire into God as into a place where they are kept in secret. On the twice-repeated prayer to be held up, Henry states the doctrine in a sentence worth the stanza: we stand no longer than God holds us and go no further than he carries us. John Gill reads the dismissal of the evildoers typologically, as words that will be spoken again at the last account; Ellicott reads it corporately, as a nation trying to purify itself of an evil influence; Clarke quotes a Latin tag about abominating the profane crowd and keeping clear of it.

The verb rendered trodden down at the end sets Ellicott off on the finest philological note in the psalm. Two old versions render it thou despisest, one has thou hast impaled and another thou hast convicted; and the word, he says, seems literally to mean to weigh or value, taking its harsher sense from the buyer’s habit of beating down a price by depreciating what he is offered — for which he compares the English word cheapen, which once meant only to buy. On the clause that follows he differs from the others as well: where John Wesley takes it that their deceitful devices will bring on themselves the destruction they designed for others, and Clarke that their elevation is a lie, Ellicott argues from the parallelism that their tricks are simply in vain, and paraphrases that their wiles are as fruitless as they are deceitful. On the dross of the next verse three of them work the metallurgy. Clarke sees the scum swept off the surface of melting metal before it is cast into the mould, Henry the dross which seems in the ore to be of the same substance as the metal and must nonetheless be separated, and Gill the hypocrites who passed for gold and were reprobate silver.
121:
This stanza produces the one disagreement in the psalm that can be settled by counting. Adam Clarke, who claimed at the outset that one of the ten names for the revelation stands in every verse but one, reports here that neither of the first two verses of this section contains any of them, since the judgment and justice of the first refer to the speaker’s own conduct and the second has no such word at all. Charles Ellicott gives a different tally on the same page, that the hundred and twenty-second and one other verse later in the psalm are the only two which do not actually mention the law under one of its terms. Clarke had already named a third verse earlier in the psalm as lacking one, so the two lists cannot both be right.

On the request to be gone surety, Clarke breaks into exclamation: be bail for thy servant — what a word is this! — pledge thyself for me that thou wilt produce me safely at the judgment of the great day. Ellicott supplies three parallels, a brother standing surety for a younger brother, a king asking God to undertake for him against the threat of death, and a sufferer summoning God as the only possible guarantee of his innocence. John Gill reports that the versions divide here, one ancient translation and two Jewish commentators reading it as a prayer that the servant be delighted with good things, while two others and two Greek translators take it as suretyship; he then develops the second at length as the office of Christ. C.H. Spurgeon defends the plea of the opening verse against the charge of self-righteousness, and does it carefully: when we deal with God about our shortcomings we use a very different tone from the one we use before the censures of our fellow men, and when men are in question and we are guiltless toward them we are justified in pleading our innocence. He adds that among eastern rulers some gave neither judgment nor justice and others judgment without justice, many selling their sentences to the highest bidder.

The famous verse near the end of the stanza can be turned round, and two of them turn it. Gill reports that it may be rendered it is time to work for the Lord, and that an ancient version and an Aramaic paraphrase agree; Matthew Henry says the original will bear the same, that it is time for every one in his place to appear on the Lord’s side, and he endorses the reading — we must do what we can for the support of the sinking interests of religion, and after all must beg God to take the work into his own hands. Henry also draws the sharpest distinction in the stanza about what the wicked have done: a godly man may sin against the commandment, but a wicked man would sin away the commandment, repealing God’s laws and enacting his own lusts. John Wesley says the same more briefly, that they have abrogated the law and openly cast off its authority. Gill adds that it was always a notion among the Jews that the Messiah would come at a time of great wickedness. On the verse that follows, Gill and Ellicott converge: the love of the commandments was the more inflamed by the contempt others had for them, and Ellicott quotes a line of English verse about one found faithful among the faithless. Keil and Delitzsch note in passing that the two nouns of the opening verse stand here in the reverse of their usual order.
129:
On the word rendered wonderful Keil and Delitzsch supply the sharpest gloss, that the testimonies are strange and paradoxical things, exalted above every-day life and the common understanding. Matthew Henry lists the grounds of the wonder — the majesty of the style, the purity of the matter, the harmony of the parts — and turns it into a test, that it is a sign we are not acquainted with these testimonies if we do not admire them. C.H. Spurgeon adds a caution about what admiration is for: some men wonder at the words of God and use them for speculation, but this writer was always practical, and the more he wondered the more he obeyed. Adam Clarke keeps the dimensions, that there is a height and length and depth in them truly astonishing, and that the more he studies the more light he obtains.

The next verse turns on a single noun, and it is taken five ways. John Gill begins with the literal beginning, since the first chapters of the Bible give such light on the origin of all things, the innocence of man and his fall and recovery; then allows that the words entering the heart is meant; then reports that it may be rendered the opening of thy words, in which case it means the interpretation and explanation of scripture by its ministers. Henry gives the same three and adds a fourth, that some understand it of the later covenant as the unfolding of the earlier. Charles Ellicott renders it literally opening and prefers the older versions’ manifestation or declaration. Clarke makes it a personal act rather than a book or a doctrine: when he opens his Bible to read, light springs up in his mind, and every sermon, every prayer, every act of faith is an opening by which light is let into the seeking soul.

The panting of the following verse is given three physical settings. Gill has a man out of breath from walking or running, or a hungry man opening his mouth before food can be brought. Henry has one overcome by heat and almost stifled, panting for a mouthful of fresh air. Clarke reverses the direction entirely: the metaphor is taken from an animal exhausted in the chase, running open-mouthed to take in the cooling air with its heart beating high and its strength nearly spent, so that the man seeks salvation as he would run from a ferocious beast for his life. On the appeal to God’s customary dealings Ellicott rejects both the received rendering and the marginal correction, and would read according to the right of those who love his name, since what they receive is theirs not merely by custom but by covenant; Henry keeps the custom and says the speaker desires no more and no better than his neighbours’ fare. Ellicott then produces an etymological curiosity at the prayer against the dominion of sin, that the cognate root of the verb in a neighbouring language gives the title sultan. On the oppression of man in the next verse Gill reports three Jewish readings that turn the request inward, one taking it as the oppression of the first man, another as the sin of that man from which the Lord’s people are redeemed, and a third as the corruption of nature that oppresses men — where Henry and Clarke take it plainly of enemies who can be told they are but men. John Wesley keeps to the surface throughout, glossing the wonder as deep mysteries and the panting as thirst.
137:
C.H. Spurgeon notices that this section’s governing letter sounds like the Hebrew word for righteousness, so that the keynote is set by the alphabet itself. He also remarks on the divine name used here, that it appears rarely in so vast a composition, since men thoroughly familiar with the things of God never use that name carelessly nor as often as the thoughtless do — familiarity, in this case, begetting reverence. Charles Ellicott supplies a historical association for the same verse, referring the reader to a historian’s account of the death of an emperor who died with these words on his lips. Ellicott then does something no one else does in this acrostic psalm: he moves a word across a verse boundary. Taking the verb commandest back into the first verse, he obtains what he calls the simple and obvious sense, that God is righteous and upright in the judgments he has commanded, and that his testimonies are righteous and faithful to the uttermost; and he says another arrangement of the text is unquestionably correct.

The word rendered pure is turned from passive to active by Adam Clarke. It is purification, he says, not a purified thing but a thing that purifies; the word is a fire to purify as well as a hammer to break, and he quotes the saying that the disciples were made clean by a word spoken to them. Ellicott keeps the passive and sharpens it, rendering it more literally purged by trial and noting that the older versions have fired, so that it is not merely the excellence but the proved excellence of the word that is loved. John Gill takes the same passive line with silver tried in a furnace and purified seven times, and John Wesley compresses it to being without the least mixture of falsehood. On the zeal of the preceding verse Matthew Henry draws a rule from what it costs: zeal against sin should constrain us to do what we can against it in our places, and at the least to do so much the more in religion ourselves, since the worse others are the better we should be.

The confession of being small and despised divides them further than anything else here. Gill reports a rendering that makes the word young and refers it to the time before the speaker’s anointing, though he prefers to take it of condition rather than age; Keil and Delitzsch keep young. Henry makes it a portrait of a man at once pious and poor, whose excellency could not secure him from contempt and indeed exposed him to it. Clarke draws the practical consequence, that being small he cannot resist and being despised he is in danger. Ellicott alone denies that an individual is meant at all, holding the words hardly applicable to one man while peculiarly suitable to a small nation standing among the great powers of the east. On the everlasting righteousness of the next verse Clarke and Gill converge on a forensic sense, Clarke observing that the word covers not only God’s inherent perfection but his method of treating others and his plan of redemption, and Gill making it the righteousness imputed to the believer; Henry keeps it as rule and standard instead, and ends with a sentence that binds the stanza together, that God’s truth is a law and God’s law is the truth, so that we cannot break such words asunder.
145:
C.H. Spurgeon lays the stanza out as a set of eight answers, one to a verse: how he prayed, what he prayed for, when he prayed, how long he prayed, what he pleaded, what happened, how he was rescued, and what his witness was about the whole matter. On the first of these he insists that heart-cries are the essence of prayer, and that there may be no beauty of elocution about such prayers, no length of expression, no depth of doctrine nor accuracy of diction, yet if the whole heart be in them they will find their way to the heart of God; he adds the maxim that he who has been with God in the closet will find God with him in the furnace. Matthew Henry puts the same negatively, that lip-labour, if that be all, is lost labour, and warns against thinking we shall be heard for much speaking, the petition here being short but comprehensive. Adam Clarke promises that whoever cries with his whole heart will never rise from the throne of grace without a blessing.

The hours of these prayers give the two textual voices something to dispute. Charles Ellicott observes that the word rendered dawning means literally breath, and is used of the fresh breeze that blows at sunset as well as at sunrise, being generally rendered twilight; so the verse does not by itself say which twilight is meant. Clarke keeps the received sense and renders it going before the dawn, and Keil and Delitzsch agree that the morning twilight is meant while denying that the verb means anticipating it. Clarke then supplies the timekeeping behind the second verse: the night was divided into three watches of four hours each beginning at six in the evening, until the Romans taught a division into four watches of three hours, and at the proclaiming of each watch the psalmist appears to have risen and performed some act of devotion — and Clarke promises a remarkable custom of our own ancestors when he reaches a later verse of this psalm. Henry draws a simpler moral, that the speaker was an early riser, which perhaps contributed to his eminence, and that he was none of those who say yet a little sleep; and he adds that if our first thoughts in the morning be of God they will help keep us in his fear all day.

On the plea in the next verse the three of them give three senses. Henry takes the word for God’s wisdom, since he knows what we need, or else for his promise. John Wesley makes it simply the word. Ellicott holds that the noun must certainly here bear the meaning of a custom, and cites with approval the old liturgical rendering, according as thou art wont. The close of the stanza turns on one antithesis, and all of them catch it. John Gill has the pursuers drawing near like huntsmen after their sport, so that the speaker’s life drew nigh to his destroyers; and then grades the nearness of God into four kinds, of relation, of union, of communion and of gracious presence. Clarke states it in a line, that as they are near to destroy, so is God near to save. Henry sharpens the comparison, that God is not only mightier than they and therefore able to help, but nearer than they and therefore ready; and he observes that God brings us into such perils, as he did the patriarch, in order that we may wrestle for a blessing.
153:
C.H. Spurgeon finds the key-word of the stanza in its first verb, and notices that there is no impatience in it: the speaker does not ask for hasty action but for consideration, in effect asking God to look into his grief and judge from it what method and time of rescue would be proper. Spurgeon also calls the two words for the affliction picturesque, since they portion off a special spot of woe as the writer’s own inheritance, possessed as no one else had ever possessed it. Matthew Henry catches the same care in the later verse where the plea is repeated, and marks precisely what is not said: he does not ask God to consider how he fulfils the precepts, being conscious that in many things he came short, but how he loves them — obedience being pleasing to God and pleasant to ourselves only when it comes from a principle of love.

On the salvation that stands far from the wicked, John Gill distinguishes several distances at once, that its author is far from them, the word of it far, an experimental knowledge of it far, and the enjoyment of it in heaven far. Adam Clarke is unusually severe, saying flatly that there is no hope of their conversion, and that those who do not seek shall not find. Henry makes the distance a moving one: they flatter themselves that salvation is near, but they thrust it from them by thrusting the Saviour from them, and the longer they persist the further it is, while damnation meanwhile comes nearer. On the mercies of the following verse Henry allows what the previous one might seem to deny, that there were tender mercies sufficient in God to have saved even those, had they not despised the riches of them.

The strongest disagreement in the stanza is about a feeling. Charles Ellicott holds that the word rendered grieved is far stronger than that, and intensified further by a rare conjugation, so that the sense is being filled with loathing and sickened with disgust; and he quotes a modern hymn-writer’s couplet about surveying the recreants and loathing to turn away. Gill and Henry both keep sorrow, Gill adding that the grief was less for the injuries done him than for the ruin the transgressors brought on themselves and the dishonour done to God; Clarke renders it simply that he was affected with anguish. On the noun itself Ellicott and Gill converge where they differed on the verb, both taking it of the treacherous rather than of open sinners; Gill notes that it may reach professors of religion who walked unagreeably to their profession. The last verse is a crux, and two of them note the alternative rendering that would make it the sum or the beginning of God’s word that is truth. Henry then produces the most unexpected citation in the psalm, a maxim of the civil law that what at first wanted validity acquires it in the progress of time; many governments, he says, have no better plea than long usage, but the word of God did not gain its validity by lapse of time, its beginning being true and its foundation sure from the first; John Wesley reads the phrase plainly, of the beginning of the world. Keil and Delitzsch ground the prayer against persecutors in the impossibility that God should let those faithful to his word succumb.
161:
The stanza opens with persecution by rulers, and the answer to it is that one fear displaced another. C.H. Spurgeon puts it exactly so, that a greater fear drove out the less, and adds that princes are appointed to protect the innocent and avenge the oppressed, so that it is a shame when they become the assailants of the righteous. Matthew Henry makes the aggravation legal: rulers not only have the sword and can therefore do more hurt, but have the law on their side and can do it with reputation and a colour of justice. John Wesley compresses the whole verse into a comparison of displeasures. Charles Ellicott reads it as another indication of the psalm’s national character, since it was a whole community that suffered from the intrigues and violence of princes. Adam Clarke applies the hatred of lying two verses later to the same situation, and gives it a sharp point: those under pressure might have made the confessions their captors required and kept by mental reservation an inward adherence to their own creed, but in the sight of the God of truth that would have been lying, and they would not purchase their release at such a price.

On the joy compared to finding great spoil, Clarke is the most concrete and the grimmest, taking it of the spoil acquired by stripping the dead on a field of battle and taking the rich garments of the slain chiefs. Henry keeps the figure but works its logic, that the comparison supposes a victory already won, and that besides the pleasure and honour of conquest there is the further advantage of the plunder. He also notices what stands on either side of the verse, that the speaker has just said his heart stood in awe of the word and now says he rejoices in it, and concludes that the more reverence we have for it the more joy we shall find in it. John Gill adds that the word is itself a part of the armour by which the victory is won.

Whether the seven daily praises are to be counted is disputed. Gill, Henry and Wesley all take the number for an indefinite one meaning very often, and Ellicott reports that some commentators do the same, though he observes that seven evidently had a sacred association. Clarke gives both, allowing the general sense but reporting a rabbinic authority who took it literally and distributed the seven around the two daily readings of the commandments; and Clarke and Ellicott agree that the canonical hours of the later church were partly derived from this verse. Clarke then produces the most remarkable thing in the psalm, redeeming a promise he had made two stanzas earlier: from a manuscript homily in the old English tongue, dated in the tenth century, he gives the sevenfold rule prescribed to every Christian man — at daybreak, at the third hour of the morning, at midday, at the ninth hour, in the evening, at night before rest, and at midnight if he should wake — adding the dry note that the sign of the cross was there thought sufficient even without prayer. On the promise that follows, Ellicott declines to take it as a statement of fact, since it was not the case that the faithful did not stumble, and offers instead to read it as a wish, great peace to the lovers of thy law and no stumbling-block to them, or else as describing those who love the word and find no hindrance; Henry builds an entire doctrine of security on the received sense, that no event of providence shall be either an invincible temptation or an intolerable affliction to such men. Keil and Delitzsch sum the stanza in a line, that in the midst of persecution the word was still his fear, his joy and his love.
169:
Both of the voices who notice the figure of the opening verse call it a personification, and each supplies a different picture for it. Adam Clarke says it is really a fine image, of frequent occurrence and little heeded: the cry for deliverance is made an intelligent being and sent up to the throne of grace to negotiate on the suppliant’s behalf, and the same is done with the supplication in the next verse; he compares the figure in the Greek epic where prayers are represented as the daughters of the chief god. C.H. Spurgeon personifies it too, and pictures the prayer as a queen venturing into the royal presence, entreating an audience and begging to find favour. Matthew Henry reads the same anxiety as a fear that the prayer may miscarry as unfit to come before God, and adds that none of our prayers would have had access if Christ had not approached as an advocate for us.

Clarke finds a curious distinction between the two verses about speech. In the first the lips utter, where no articulate sounds are meant except as attached to musical notes; in the second the tongue speaks, where intelligible words are intended. So the man first utters sounds expressive of his grateful feelings and then speaks words, chiefly those God had himself spoken. Charles Ellicott and John Gill both catch the metaphor in the first of the two, that the verb means to pour forth a stream, Gill adding that praise so described comes freely and without compulsion as water from a fountain. Ellicott then renders the second antiphonally, that the tongue shall make response to God’s word rather than speak about it. On the prayer to live a little longer Henry states the only reason he will allow: not let me live and serve my country or provide for my family, but let me live that in doing this I may praise God in a world of conflict and opposition; when we die we hope to go to a better world to praise him, which is more agreeable for us, though here there is more need of us.

The last verse turns the whole psalm round. Gill reads the straying two ways, of a sheep wandering from the fold through inadvertence and the prevalence of corruption, and of a man driven by persecution to wander from the courts of God. Henry keeps the moral sense and observes that we are apt to wander like sheep and very unapt, having gone astray, to find the way again; then he makes the request personal in a way no one else does, since the man asking to be sought had himself been a shepherd, and now asks God to seek him as he used to seek his own sheep when they went astray. Seek me, Henry adds, that is, find me, for God never seeks in vain. Spurgeon draws the shape of the ending: the nearer the psalmist comes, the lower his view of himself, so that he closes the psalm on his face in deepest self-humiliation, begging to be sought out like a lost sheep. Keil and Delitzsch pair the two petitions of the stanza and give the reason they go together, that a man persecuted for his faith needs the fortifying of that faith as much as deliverance from what restrains him. Henry ends where the psalm does, that a devout man will conclude his duties and conclude his life the same way, living and dying repenting and praying. John Wesley leaves the last word with the text itself, which he calls the only ground of his hope in God’s help.
